name: Kilo Code
summary: An open-source agentic engineering platform and coding agent forked from OpenCode, with shared Effect services for sessions, tools, plugins, model providers, compaction, and multiple IDE/CLI surfaces.
scope: VS Code, JetBrains, CLI, and cloud integration surfaces

features.name: Multi-surface coding-agent platform
features.description: The official README describes Kilo as an open-source coding agent for VS Code, JetBrains, and CLI, with additional cloud, code-review, marketplace, and multi-model surfaces; the repository contains corresponding packages and platform tooling.
benefits: Presents one agent product across common developer surfaces
Allows local and hosted workflows to share agent concepts
costs: Platform-specific integrations expand release and compatibility matrices
A shared product contract must accommodate IDE, CLI, and hosted capabilities

features.name: Durable session runner with tool settlement
features.description: The Kilo core session runner loads session context, resolves agents and models, streams provider turns, records tool calls, settles local tool fibers, persists typed events, and continues across steps with optional agent limits.
benefits: Tool execution and provider output have explicit durable boundaries
The loop can recover and continue after tool settlement or compaction
costs: Durable event and tool state require database and concurrency coordination
Provider and local execution failure modes must be reconciled

features.name: Policy-filtered built-in, MCP, plugin, and structured tools
features.description: Kilo materializes tools from a registry and agent permissions, while the repository provides built-in filesystem/shell tools, MCP and plugin integration, and tool-output persistence around session execution.
benefits: The same agent runtime can expose different tool loadouts
Permission and registry boundaries make tool availability configurable
costs: Tool policies and external integrations increase authorization surface
Tool materialization can vary by agent, step, and provider capability

features.name: Model-provider and plugin composition
features.description: Kilo retains OpenCode-style provider/plugin boundaries and adds Kilo gateway, indexing, sandbox, board, and session components through workspace packages and core services.
benefits: Provider and product integrations can evolve behind service boundaries
Plugins can add commands, agents, providers, and skills without rewriting the session loop
costs: Fork-specific extensions increase divergence and integration maintenance
Plugin activation and provider routing are additional runtime state

mathematical_views.question: How do Kilo's CLI/IDE surfaces, core session services, provider routes, tools, plugins, and product packages connect?
assumptions: Packages and services are graph vertices and imports/registrations are directed edges
The graph abstracts UI event loops and network transport
A fork relationship is provenance, not a proof of identical behavior
External cloud services are boundary nodes rather than local implementations

mathematical_views.question: How does a Kilo session move from admitted input to provider stream, tool settlement, continuation, retry, compaction, and completion?
assumptions: Session history and events are durable projections
Tool calls are recorded before local side effects and later settled
A step limit can remove tool materialization from the final step
The model abstracts database transaction details and provider semantics

mathematical_views.question: Which built-in, MCP, plugin, and structured-output tools are exposed for an agent and step?
assumptions: Agent permission rules and tool registry definitions are source sets
Materialization is a projection that may depend on step and provider state
Tool availability does not establish that an invocation is safe or successful
The view excludes undocumented runtime policy outside the inspected source

benefits: One product spans IDE and terminal workflows
costs: More platform-specific build and release paths
Database and event coordination are required
Permission, MCP, and plugin interactions complicate reasoning
